Such materials, referred to as phase-change materials (PCMs), have a specific storage capacity during the phase transition process, during which energy is added or released as the material melts or solidifies, or boils or condenses. In general, PCMs are typically those with solid- to-liquid phase transitions [17], [20], [21], [26]. The reduction in volume compared to the sensible TES system primarily stems from the higher thermal energy stored in the two- phase region than the specific heat capacity of sensible TES [27]. This is evident in Figure 3, where the required energy to change phase at the phase-change temperature or within the temperature range is substantial compared to the single-phase sensible regions. Figure 3: Energy stored in the phase-change transition region compared to the single-phase region (adapted from [27] and [28]) HP-TES Integration Strategies TES integrations can be either active or passive. Active TES enables a complete intentional control of melting and solidification through a mechanical system, whereas passive systems rely solely on ambient temperatures or conditions to discharge and charge [29]. Examples of passive TES integrations include the pre-cooling of outdoor air around the condenser (Figure 4), as described by Said & Hassan [30], to lower the temperature lift during the vapor compression cycle during high-temperature hours. In this case, the PCM is discharged and melted using outdoor hot air, and then recharged in cooler nocturnal ambient conditions. Another example of a passive system was proposed by Chaiyat & Kiatsiriroat [31], in which the recirculated room air was pre-cooled before Page 9 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park mixing with the ventilation air. In this case, warm room-temperature return air melts the PCM during peak hours, and cooled off-coil supply air is used to solidify the PCM. In both examples, PCM integration techniques were passively implemented to limit HP operating hours during high-demand periods, thereby reducing grid power draw. Figure 4: Passive HP-TES systems: precooling condenser air (left, Said & Hassan [30]), and pre- cooling mixed air (right, Chaiyat & Kiatsiriroat [31]) As passive systems are limited in their applications and potential, there is a greater focus on active systems [15], [32] due to their flexibility and higher peak-shaving potential. Active HP-TES systems utilize mechanical components and controls to operate the TES, achieving higher peak energy reductions due to more flexible system architectures [17], [33] and more robust control strategies [34]. Active HP-TES system concepts exist in several configurations, depending on the location and the application. Cooling-specific HP-TES applications usually use a low-temperature PCM (e.g., ice) as a heat sink or directly to cool a space (Figure 5(a)). On the other hand, heating-specific utilizes a high- temperature heat source (Figure 5(b)).
